title: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?

title: How would you diagnose a slow Spring Boot endpoint?
short: Start with measurements across request handling, database, downstream calls, thread pools and serialization.
answer: I would correlate the request with logs and traces, inspect latency percentiles and identify whether time is spent in application code, SQL, remote calls, thread-pool queues or GC. Then I would reproduce the bottleneck and change one variable at a time.

interview: I first measure the endpoint end to end, then break latency down using metrics, logs, traces and SQL timings. The fix depends on the bottleneck rather than assumptions.

title: What is Spring application event publishing?
short: Spring events let components publish an application-level event and other beans react to it.

interview: Spring application events are in-process notifications, not a durable messaging system. For cross-service reliability I would use a broker and an appropriate delivery pattern.

title: How does @Async work?
short: @Async runs eligible method calls on a task executor instead of the caller thread.

interview: @Async moves work to a configured executor through Spring interception. I size and monitor the executor for the workload and handle errors explicitly.

title: How would you design API versioning?

interview: I prefer backward-compatible evolution first. For breaking changes, I use an explicit versioning strategy, support overlap, measure usage and communicate deprecation before retirement.

title: Explain the Spring three-level singleton cache

Dependency checks should be used thoughtfully because a transient dependency outage should not necessarily restart every pod.
mistakes: Using dependency failure as a liveness condition.
interview: I keep liveness cheap and readiness traffic-oriented. I do not put fragile downstream checks into liveness because that can create restart storms.

title: How do you design Spring async processing safely?
short: Use bounded executors, explicit error handling and durable state for work that must survive process failure.
answer: @Async is thread-based and context such as transactions does not automatically move to another thread. Configure named executors, queue limits and rejection behavior. For durable business work, prefer a queue/outbox.
followups: How do you propagate tracing context?
mistakes: Using the default executor for unbounded work.
interview: For fire-and-forget business work I prefer durable messaging. If I use @Async, I bound the executor and make failure observable.

title: How would you troubleshoot a slow Spring Boot endpoint?
short: Break total latency into application, database, serialization and downstream components using traces and metrics.
answer: Inspect p50/p95/p99, DB timings, connection-pool wait, downstream spans, payload sizes and thread states. Look for N+1 queries, lock waits and pool saturation before changing code.
code: // Trace: controller -> service -> DB -> downstream -> serialization
followups: How do you detect pool exhaustion?
mistakes: Adding async just to hide latency.
interview: I optimize the largest measured contributor. A slow endpoint is often a DB or downstream problem rather than a slow Java method.

title: How do you perform zero-downtime Spring/database deployments?
short: Make application versions compatible with the database during rolling deployment.
answer: Use expand-and-contract: add compatible schema, deploy code supporting both shapes, backfill, switch reads/writes, then remove the old shape after all old instances are gone.
code: ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status_v2 VARCHAR(30);
followups: How do you backfill millions of rows?
How do you roll back code after schema expansion?
mistakes: Deploying an incompatible column rename in one release.
interview: Rolling deployment means old and new binaries coexist. Therefore database changes must be backward compatible during the whole rollout.

title: How do you design a reliable scheduled job in Spring Boot?
short: Coordinate ownership across instances and make the job idempotent and recoverable.
answer: @Scheduled runs independently in every JVM. Use a distributed scheduler/lease or durable job queue. Persist execution state and make retries safe.
followups: How do you prevent duplicate execution?
mistakes: Assuming @Scheduled executes once cluster-wide.
interview: A scheduled annotation is local to a JVM. In a cluster I need distributed ownership and recovery semantics.

title: How do you test transactional behavior in Spring?
short: Use integration tests with a production-like database for rollback, isolation, locking and lazy-loading behavior.
answer: Mocks cannot prove database transaction semantics. A disposable real database lets tests verify commit/rollback and SQL constraints across transaction boundaries.
code: // call service -> verify persisted state from a fresh transaction/context
mistakes: Relying entirely on mocked repositories.
interview: I use unit tests for business branching and integration tests for actual transaction behavior.

title: @Async tasks overwhelm the application thread pool
short: Asynchrony changes where work waits; it does not remove capacity limits.
answer: I would use a dedicated bounded executor, measure task duration and choose a rejection or backpressure policy. For durable background work I would prefer a queue so work survives process restarts.
code: Use a dedicated bounded executor with an explicit queue and rejection policy. Size it for the workload, isolate unrelated task types and move durable long-running work to a message broker when necessary.
followups: How do you size a thread pool?
What happens when the executor queue is full?
When would Kafka be better than @Async?
mistakes: Using an unbounded queue.
Sharing one executor across unrelated workloads.
interview: I would not solve this by simply increasing the thread count. I would bound the executor and choose whether excess work should be rejected, delayed or persisted to messaging.
scenario: A new asynchronous feature submits thousands of tasks. The default executor queue grows, memory increases and request latency degrades.
investigation: Inspect executor active threads, queue depth, task duration and rejection count. Check whether tasks are CPU-bound or I/O-bound and whether callers need the work synchronously.
resolution: Use a dedicated bounded executor with an explicit queue and rejection policy. Size it for the workload, isolate unrelated task types and move durable long-running work to a message broker when necessary.
prevention: Monitor executor saturation and load-test bursts. Do not use one unbounded executor for unrelated workloads.

title: A transactional method calls an @Async method and data is missing
short: Spring transactions are thread-bound; asynchronous execution creates a different execution context.
answer: I would not rely on the async method seeing uncommitted transaction state. If the task needs committed data, I would trigger it after commit or use a durable event/message so the ordering is explicit.
code: Do not assume @Async inherits the transaction. Publish an event after commit or move the asynchronous work behind a durable queue. If direct async execution is acceptable, ensure the transaction has committed before the async work starts.
followups: How does @Transactional interact with thread pools?
How would you publish an event after commit?
mistakes: Assuming @Async inherits the transaction.
Starting background work before commit.
interview: A transaction does not automatically flow into @Async. Crossing the thread boundary means I need an explicit post-commit or messaging design.
scenario: A service saves an entity inside a transaction and then calls an asynchronous method that immediately queries the database. The async task sometimes cannot see the expected data.
investigation: Check transaction commit timing and thread boundaries. @Async executes on another thread, so it does not share the caller thread-bound transaction.
resolution: Do not assume @Async inherits the transaction. Publish an event after commit or move the asynchronous work behind a durable queue. If direct async execution is acceptable, ensure the transaction has committed before the async work starts.
prevention: Test commit/async race conditions and define whether the background task requires committed state or can operate on an in-memory command.

title: A Spring Boot application starts slowly after a new release
short: Startup performance should be measured by phase; otherwise teams tend to guess which bean is responsible.
answer: I would profile startup and compare bean initialization and external calls with the previous version. Then I would move non-critical work out of startup and reduce scanning or initialization only where measurements justify it.
code: Remove unnecessary scanning, defer non-critical initialization and move expensive startup work out of the critical path. Use lazy initialization selectively, not as a blanket fix.
followups: How does Spring Boot auto-configuration affect startup?
How would you debug a startup hang?
mistakes: Enabling lazy initialization everywhere without measuring.
Ignoring external calls during startup.
interview: I would profile first, because startup can be slow due to bean creation, database migration, classpath scanning or remote configuration.
scenario: Startup time increases from 15 seconds to 90 seconds after adding several dependencies and configuration classes.
investigation: Compare startup profiles between releases. Inspect bean creation, classpath scanning, database initialization, remote configuration and slow post-construct/startup tasks.
resolution: Remove unnecessary scanning, defer non-critical initialization and move expensive startup work out of the critical path. Use lazy initialization selectively, not as a blanket fix.
prevention: Track startup time as a deployment metric and keep startup dependencies deterministic. Profile before optimizing.

title: A controller returns 200 but the business operation failed
short: An HTTP success response is part of the business contract; swallowing failures can be worse than returning a 500.
answer: I would avoid catching exceptions merely to log them. Unexpected failures should reach centralized exception handling, which returns a consistent status and error body. Known business errors should map explicitly to meaningful 4xx responses.
code: Let unexpected exceptions propagate to a centralized exception handler and map them to appropriate status codes. Return a stable error contract with correlation information, not internal stack traces.
followups: When should a business error be 409 versus 400?
How do you avoid leaking stack traces?
How do you correlate errors across services?
mistakes: Returning 200 with an error message.
Logging and swallowing exceptions.
interview: I want HTTP status to reflect the actual outcome. Centralized exception handling gives consistent client behavior and keeps controllers focused on business flow.
scenario: An endpoint catches an exception, logs it and returns a default response, so clients believe the operation succeeded.
investigation: Trace the exception path and inspect HTTP status mapping. Check whether global exception handling is bypassed by local catches.
resolution: Let unexpected exceptions propagate to a centralized exception handler and map them to appropriate status codes. Return a stable error contract with correlation information, not internal stack traces.
prevention: Define an error-response standard, test failure status codes and alert on unexpected 5xx rates rather than only application exceptions.

title: A memory leak appears after adding request caching
short: A cache without bounded cardinality is a memory leak from the application perspective even if every entry is technically reachable.
answer: I would confirm the retaining path with a heap dump, then inspect cache cardinality and eviction. The fix is to bound the cache and avoid storing large request objects, not simply increase heap size.
code: Bound the cache by size and TTL, store only the data required for reuse and avoid retaining request-scoped objects. If the data needs distributed durability, use an external cache with explicit eviction.
followups: How do you take a heap dump safely?
How do you distinguish a leak from normal heap growth?
What GC metrics would you monitor?
mistakes: Increasing heap size without finding the retaining object.
Using an unbounded map as a cache.
interview: I would use heap analysis to prove what is retaining memory, then bound the cache by size and lifetime.
scenario: Heap usage grows continuously in production even after traffic returns to normal. A new in-memory cache stores request-derived objects.
investigation: Use heap dumps and allocation profiling. Identify the retaining path and cache size, eviction policy and key cardinality. Check whether user/request objects are referenced longer than intended.
resolution: Bound the cache by size and TTL, store only the data required for reuse and avoid retaining request-scoped objects. If the data needs distributed durability, use an external cache with explicit eviction.
prevention: Monitor heap occupancy and cache cardinality, test long-running workloads and set memory alerts before the process reaches OOM.

title: Spring Security allows an endpoint that should be admin-only
short: Authentication proves identity; authorization decides whether that identity can perform the operation.
answer: I would verify the filter-chain rule and method-security configuration, then test the endpoint with users having different authorities. Authorization should be enforced server-side and covered by integration tests.
code: Define authorization at the correct layer and use explicit authorities/roles consistently. Add integration tests that assert both allowed and forbidden users receive the expected status.
followups: Role versus authority in Spring Security?
How do you test forbidden access?
mistakes: Checking permissions only in the frontend.
Mixing ROLE_ADMIN and ADMIN conventions.
interview: I would debug authorization from the token claims through the filter chain to the method decision, not just inspect the annotation.
scenario: An endpoint is protected by authentication, but any logged-in user can call it because the method-level role check was not applied as expected.
investigation: Inspect the filter chain, endpoint matchers, method-security configuration and exact authority names. Verify whether the call is going through a proxy and whether annotations are enabled.
resolution: Define authorization at the correct layer and use explicit authorities/roles consistently. Add integration tests that assert both allowed and forbidden users receive the expected status.
prevention: Treat authorization tests as security regression tests. Avoid relying on controller visibility or UI restrictions.

title: Database connection pool is exhausted under moderate traffic
short: A connection pool can be exhausted because connections are held too long, not because the database itself is at CPU capacity.
answer: I would check pool acquisition latency and active connection age. Then I would look for slow SQL or transactions that include remote calls. Increasing the pool blindly may move the bottleneck to the database and increase contention.
followups: How do you choose HikariCP pool size?
mistakes: Do not increase pool size without measuring database capacity.
interview: The important distinction is database capacity versus application-side connection occupancy.
scenario: Requests start timing out waiting for database connections, even though database CPU is only 40%.
investigation: Inspect active/idle pool counts, connection acquisition time, slow queries, long transactions and leaked connections. Compare application thread count with pool size.
prevention: Fix slow queries and transaction scope first. Configure sensible pool limits and leak detection, avoid holding connections across remote calls, and monitor acquisition latency.

title: Spring @Async work never runs asynchronously
short: @Async is proxy-based. A direct self-invocation bypasses the proxy and therefore bypasses asynchronous interception.
answer: I would first confirm the executor and proxy path. If the method is called from another method in the same class, I would move the async operation behind another bean or otherwise ensure the invocation crosses the Spring proxy. I would also configure a bounded executor rather than relying on an unbounded default.
followups: How would you propagate MDC or security context?
mistakes: Do not assume an annotation changes execution without proxy interception.
interview: Async is not a magic annotation; proxy interception and executor capacity are both part of the design.
scenario: A method annotated with @Async executes on the caller thread in production.
investigation: Check whether @EnableAsync is configured, whether the method is public, whether the call goes through a Spring proxy, and whether the executor is configured. Look for self-invocation.
prevention: Call the async method through a Spring-managed proxy, configure a bounded executor, propagate required context explicitly, and monitor queue saturation.

title: Spring transaction does not roll back after an exception
short: Spring rollback is based on transaction interception and rollback rules. Catching an exception without marking rollback can allow the transaction to commit.
answer: I would verify the transaction boundary first. If the exception is caught inside the transaction and swallowed, I would either rethrow it or mark the transaction rollback-only. For checked exceptions I would explicitly configure rollback behavior when that matches the business requirement.
mistakes: Do not assume checked exceptions always trigger rollback.
interview: The key is that @Transactional controls a transaction boundary; it does not automatically roll back every exception that ever occurred inside the method.
scenario: A service method annotated with @Transactional catches an exception and returns normally, but the caller expects the database changes to roll back.
investigation: Inspect whether the exception was caught inside the transactional method, whether the exception type matches Spring rollback rules, and whether the call entered through a transaction proxy.
prevention: Let the intended exception propagate or explicitly mark the transaction rollback-only. Configure rollbackFor for checked exceptions when appropriate and avoid self-invocation of transactional methods.

title: Spring application startup becomes much slower after adding a module
short: Slow startup often comes from expensive bean initialization or unnecessary scanning rather than Spring Boot itself.
answer: I would measure startup phases and identify the slow bean or auto-configuration. I would then remove external calls from constructors or initialization paths and reduce unnecessary scanning. I would not optimize startup blindly without a measurement.
followups: How would you troubleshoot a circular dependency?
mistakes: Do not disable broad auto-configurations without understanding what they provide.
interview: Production startup matters for autoscaling and rolling deployments, so startup time is an operational metric.
scenario: Startup time increases from 10 seconds to 45 seconds after a dependency and several configuration classes are added.
investigation: Enable startup metrics or a startup actuator endpoint where appropriate, inspect bean initialization, auto-configuration reports, external calls during bean creation and classpath scanning.
prevention: Avoid network calls during bean construction, reduce unnecessary component scanning, exclude irrelevant auto-configurations when justified, and move expensive work to controlled initialization or asynchronous workflows.

title: Spring REST endpoint returns 500 because validation exceptions bypass the global handler
short: Validation failures should normally be translated into a consistent client-facing 4xx response rather than leaking as 500 errors.
answer: I would inspect the actual exception type first. Then I would add a targeted global handler for validation and binding failures and return a stable error format with field-level messages. I would add integration tests so every controller follows the same contract.
followups: How do you validate path variables?
How do you avoid exposing internal exception messages?
mistakes: Do not return stack traces to clients.
interview: Do not assume every validation failure arrives as MethodArgumentNotValidException; the exact exception depends on how validation is triggered.
scenario: Invalid request payloads sometimes produce inconsistent 400/500 responses depending on the controller.
investigation: Inspect exception types thrown by request binding/validation and compare them with the @ControllerAdvice handlers. Verify whether handler methods cover the actual framework exception types.
prevention: Define a consistent error contract, handle validation/binding exceptions centrally, and test malformed payloads across controllers.

title: Spring cache serves stale data after an update
short: Caching introduces a second copy of data, so the application must define how and when that copy becomes stale.
answer: I would first verify whether the write invalidates the exact cache key after the database transaction succeeds. In a multi-instance system I would prefer a shared cache or an invalidation mechanism rather than assuming local caches are consistent.
followups: How do you prevent cache stampede?
What happens if the cache is unavailable?
mistakes: Do not invalidate the cache before a failed database write unless the policy is deliberate.
interview: Cache consistency is a business trade-off. The interview answer should state the acceptable staleness requirement.
scenario: An update succeeds in the database, but subsequent GET requests still return the old value from the cache.
investigation: Check cache eviction/update semantics, transaction timing, cache key consistency and whether multiple application instances maintain independent local caches.
prevention: Use a clear cache-aside policy, evict or update the cache after a successful write, and use a shared cache when cross-instance consistency is required. Define an acceptable staleness window.

title: How does Spring resolve bean dependencies?
short: Spring resolves required beans from the ApplicationContext using type, qualifiers, primary candidates and other metadata.
answer: Dependency resolution considers type and qualifiers and can fail on ambiguity or missing beans. Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and supports immutable components.
followups: What happens with two beans of the same type?
interview: I prefer constructor injection because dependencies are explicit and the object cannot be created without them. Qualifier or primary resolves intentional ambiguity.

title: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
short: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit and supports immutability and easier testing.
answer: The object can be instantiated with all required collaborators, fields can be final, and missing dependencies fail early. Field injection hides dependencies and complicates plain unit tests.
interview: For required dependencies I use constructors. It improves design and makes the class valid immediately after construction.

title: How does Spring handle circular dependencies?
short: A circular dependency occurs when bean A requires B while B requires A.
answer: Some setter/field injection cases can be resolved through early references, but constructor cycles cannot be satisfied normally. The best fix is usually redesigning responsibilities rather than relying on lazy workarounds.
interview: I treat circular dependencies as a design smell. I first split responsibilities or introduce a domain service rather than hiding the cycle with @Lazy.

title: What is BeanPostProcessor?
short: BeanPostProcessor hooks into bean creation before and after initialization.
answer: Spring uses post-processors for concerns such as dependency injection, annotation processing and proxy creation. This is a major extension point in the container lifecycle.
interview: BeanPostProcessor lets Spring inspect or wrap beans during creation. Many framework features are implemented through these lifecycle extension points.
scenario: BeanPostProcessor hooks into bean creation before and after initialization.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: What is BeanFactoryPostProcessor?
short: It can modify bean definitions before regular beans are instantiated.
answer: It operates on metadata rather than bean instances. This distinction is important when understanding configuration processing and how Spring prepares the container.
interview: BeanFactoryPostProcessor changes bean definitions before bean instantiation; BeanPostProcessor works with bean instances during lifecycle processing.

title: How does @Lazy affect Spring bean creation?
short: @Lazy defers bean creation until it is first needed.
answer: It can reduce startup cost but moves initialization latency to first use and can hide configuration errors until runtime. It should not be used to paper over dependency design problems.
followups: When is it a bad idea?
interview: Lazy initialization can improve startup, but it trades startup work for first-use latency and delayed failures.

title: How does Spring's transaction interceptor decide commit or rollback?
short: The transaction interceptor starts or joins a transaction, invokes the target, then commits or rolls back based on outcome and rollback rules.
answer: By default, runtime exceptions and errors trigger rollback in typical declarative transaction handling, while checked exceptions may require explicit rollback configuration. The actual behavior depends on the transaction manager and rules.
followups: How do you roll back for checked exceptions?
What if an exception is caught inside the method?
interview: I explain that the proxy surrounds the method, begins or joins a transaction, and commits on successful completion or rolls back according to configured rollback rules.

title: What is read-only transaction optimization?
short: readOnly is a transaction hint indicating that the transaction is intended for reads.
answer: It can influence ORM flush behavior or database handling depending on the stack, but it is not a universal enforcement that prevents writes. It should not replace authorization or application-level rules.
interview: readOnly communicates intent and may reduce unnecessary flush work, but I don't treat it as a hard write prohibition.

title: How does Spring Retry differ from manual retries?
short: Spring Retry centralizes retry policy through annotations or interceptors.
answer: It can manage attempts, backoff and exception classification, but retrying still requires idempotency and timeout boundaries. A framework does not make unsafe operations safe to repeat.
interview: Retry policy should be explicit and bounded. Whether implemented with Spring Retry or manually, I need idempotency, backoff and a clear list of retryable failures.

title: How do you test a transactional service correctly?
short: Transactional tests should verify both database state and transaction boundaries.
answer: Use integration tests when behavior depends on real transaction semantics, rollback, isolation or JPA flush behavior. Unit tests can cover business branching without requiring a database.
interview: I use unit tests for business logic and integration tests for actual transaction behavior, especially rollback and persistence-context semantics.

title: What is Testcontainers useful for?
short: Testcontainers runs real infrastructure such as databases or brokers in disposable containers for tests.
answer: It improves fidelity compared with mocks or embedded substitutes and is valuable for SQL dialect, migrations and integration behavior.
followups: How do you keep tests fast?
interview: For persistence or messaging integration tests, Testcontainers gives me the real dependency and catches environment-specific behavior earlier.

title: How do you avoid leaking sensitive actuator information?
short: Operational endpoints can expose environment, mappings or metrics that may reveal sensitive details.
answer: Expose only required endpoints, secure them with authentication/authorization, and avoid returning secrets in configuration or error payloads. Network restrictions can provide another layer.
interview: Actuator should be treated as an operational API. I expose the minimum surface and secure sensitive endpoints separately from public application endpoints.

title: How should correlation IDs be propagated in Spring services?
short: A correlation ID links logs and traces belonging to the same request flow.
answer: Generate one at the edge if absent, validate/limit incoming values, put it into request context and propagate it to downstream calls and logs. Distributed tracing can provide richer context.
followups: How do you propagate across async execution?
interview: I establish correlation at the ingress boundary and propagate it consistently. I also ensure it cannot be used to inject arbitrary log control characters or sensitive data.

title: What is Spring's application event mechanism good for?
short: Application events decouple in-process publishers from listeners.
answer: They are useful for local domain notifications, but they are not a durable distributed message broker. If a business event must survive process failure, use durable messaging or an outbox.
followups: How do you make listeners async?
interview: Spring events are in-process. I use them for local decoupling, not as a replacement for Kafka when durability and cross-service delivery matter.

title: How does @TransactionalEventListener work?
short: It can execute a listener at a transaction phase such as after commit.
answer: This is useful when an in-process action should occur only after successful commit. It is still local to the application and can be lost if the process dies before the listener executes.
interview: For post-commit local work I can use @TransactionalEventListener, but for durable external events I prefer an outbox because application events are not a durable queue.

title: How do you handle large file uploads in Spring Boot?
short: Large uploads should avoid buffering entire files in application memory.
answer: Use streaming or multipart handling with size limits, content validation, temporary storage and preferably object storage for large payloads. Scan or validate files before making them available.
followups: How do you prevent disk exhaustion?
How do you secure uploaded files?
interview: I enforce request-size limits, stream large content, validate type and size, and use object storage rather than keeping large files in JVM memory.

title: How should pagination be implemented in a REST API?
short: Pagination limits response size and controls database work.
answer: For large mutable datasets, stable ordering plus keyset pagination is often safer than deep offsets. The API should define limits and deterministic ordering.
followups: How do you handle deleted rows?
interview: I cap page size and use deterministic ordering. For large sequential datasets I prefer keyset pagination to avoid deep OFFSET costs.

title: How do you design API idempotency in Spring Boot?
short: Idempotency keys let clients safely retry operations without creating duplicate business effects.
answer: Store a key scoped to the client and operation with a unique constraint and outcome. Handle concurrent duplicate requests atomically.
followups: What if two requests arrive simultaneously?
interview: I implement idempotency at the service boundary with a durable key and unique constraint, then return the original result for safe retries.

title: How do you handle timeouts in WebClient?
short: HTTP client calls need bounded connection, response and overall operation timeouts.
answer: A timeout should align with the end-to-end deadline and be observable. Retrying after a timeout is only safe when the operation is idempotent or otherwise protected.
followups: How do you prevent hanging connections?
interview: I set bounded timeouts at the client and propagate the request deadline. I don't treat timeout as automatically retryable because the downstream may have already processed the request.

title: How do you make scheduled Spring jobs safe in multiple instances?
short: A scheduled method runs in every application instance unless coordinated.
answer: For cluster-wide singleton work, use a distributed lock, leader election or move the job to a dedicated scheduler/queue. The job itself should also be idempotent.
followups: What if the lock holder crashes?
interview: In a horizontally scaled service I never assume @Scheduled runs once globally. I use a distributed coordination mechanism or a dedicated job runner.
scenario: A scheduled method runs in every application instance unless coordinated.
investigation: Start with metrics and traces, identify the failing boundary, compare latency/error rates and inspect resource saturation before changing configuration.
prevention: Use explicit timeouts, bounded resources, automated tests and alerts around the failure mode so the same issue is detected early.

title: How do you avoid blocking calls in a reactive Spring application?
short: Blocking work can occupy reactive event-loop threads and destroy throughput.
answer: Reactive applications rely on a small number of event-loop threads. Blocking JDBC, file I/O or long CPU work on those threads can stall unrelated requests. Blocking work should use an appropriate scheduler or, preferably, a non-blocking client.
followups: How do you detect blocking calls?
interview: In WebFlux I keep the event loop non-blocking. If a legacy blocking dependency cannot be replaced, I isolate it on a bounded scheduler and monitor its queue and latency rather than blocking event-loop threads.
